blocks.text: Git is a distributed version control system — software that tracks every change made to a set of files over time, so you can see what changed, who changed it, why (via a commit message), and roll back to any earlier point whenever you need to. It was created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 to manage the Linux kernel's source code, and is now the version control system almost every software team uses.

At its core, Git takes a snapshot of your entire project every time you commit, rather than just recording line-by-line differences. Each snapshot (commit) knows which snapshot came before it, so the full history of a project is a chain of commits you can walk backward and forward through.

code.content:
git init                 # start tracking a project with Git
git add index.html        # stage a change
git commit -m "Add homepage"  # save a snapshot with a message

blocks.title: Key takeaway
points: Git is a tool for recording the history of a project as a series of snapshots (commits), so nothing is ever truly lost and every change is attributable.
"Distributed" means every developer's clone of the repository has the full history, not just a reference to one central server — you'll see why that matters in the next topic.
